module_title: Sourcing and Quality Assessment of Raw Materials

lessons.title: Identifying optimal harvest time and drying methods
lessons.body:
Harvest hibiscus calyces when the flowers have dropped and the calyces are fully red but still slightly soft. In most African regions, this occurs 90â120 days after planting, depending on variety and rainfall. Check daily: if the calyx feels papery and the seed pod inside rattles when shaken, you are late. Overâmature calyces lose colour and flavour. The best time is early morning after dew has dried, but before the midday heat. Use sharp secateurs or a knife to cut the calyx from the stem, leaving about 1 cm of stem attached. Collect in clean baskets or cotton sacksânever plastic bags, which trap moisture and cause mould within hours.

Drying is the most critical step for quality. Spread calyces in a single layer on raised wire mesh or clean drying racks. In full sun, they dry in 2â3 days; in partial shade, 4â5 days. Turn them twice daily. Ideal drying temperature is 35â45Â°C. If you can, build a solar dryer with a blackâpainted metal tray inside a wooden box covered with clear polythene. This reaches 50â60Â°C and dries in 1â2 days, preserving deep red colour. Avoid drying on bare ground or on corrugated iron roofsâthese cause contamination and uneven drying.

Test for dryness: a fully dried calyx snaps when bent; it does not bend like leather. Moisture content should be 10â12%. You can estimate by weight: 5 kg fresh calyces yield about 1 kg dried. If you squeeze a handful and they stick together, they are not dry enough. Spread them again for another day.

After drying, remove foreign matter: leaves, stems, sand, and insects. Then store in clean, dry jute bags or airtight plastic containers. Never store in fertiliser or cement bagsâresidual chemicals ruin the product. Keep in a cool, dark room. Properly dried and stored calyces retain good colour and flavour for 12â18 months.

lessons.title: Assessing color, aroma, and moisture content of calyces
lessons.body:
Colour is your first quality indicator. Premium hibiscus calyces are deep crimson to dark red, almost burgundy. Faded, brownish, or pale pink calyces mean poor drying or old ageâthey will give weak colour and flat taste. Look for uniformity: a batch with mixed colours suggests mixed harvest times or varieties. Shake a handful; if you see lots of pale or greenish calyces, reject that portion. For a simple test, crush a few calyces in your palmâthe powder should stain your skin bright red. If it leaves only a faint pink mark, the quality is low.

Aroma should be fruity, tart, and slightly floralâlike dried cranberry or sorrel. A musty, mouldy, or dusty smell means the calyces were stored damp or contaminated. Sniff a closed handful; if the smell makes you cough or smells like old hay, do not buy. Fresh dried calyces have a sharp, clean tartness that tickles your nose. You can also chew a small piece: it should be sour and astringent, not bitter or bland.

Moisture content is critical for shelf life. Ideal is 10â12%. You can test without a meter: take a handful and squeeze hard. If calyces crumble and crack, they are dry enough. If they clump together or feel cool and clammy, they are too wet. For a more precise check, use a cheap digital moisture meter (â¦15,000ââ¦25,000 in Nigeria, or equivalent). Press the prongs into a sample; readings above 14% mean risk of mould within weeks. Alternatively, weigh 100 g of calyces, dry them in an oven at 105Â°C for 2 hours, then weigh again. If the weight drops by more than 12 g, moisture is too high.

Always check for insects: look for fine webbing, small holes, or live beetles. Sift a sample through a 2 mm sieveâany dust or frass indicates infestation. Combine colour, aroma, and moisture checks before buying. A batch that passes all three will make a concentrate with rich colour and strong tartness.

lessons.title: Detecting adulterants and contaminants
lessons.body:
Adulteration is common in African markets. Sellers may mix hibiscus with cheaper fillers like sawdust, sand, dried tomato peel, or even red dye. To detect sand and grit, put a handful of calyces in a clear glass of water. Real calyces float; sand and soil sink immediately. Stir and let settle for 2 minutes. Any sediment at the bottom is a red flag. For dye adulteration, soak calyces in cold water for 10 minutes. Natural hibiscus releases colour slowly and the water turns red gradually. If the water turns bright red instantly, suspect added dye. You can also rub a wet calyx on white paperânatural colour leaves a faint pink stain, while dye leaves a strong, unnatural red streak.

Contaminants include mould, insect parts, rodent hair, and stones. Mould appears as white, green, or black powdery patches. Smell for mustiness. Insect damage shows as small holes, webbing, or live insects. Sift through a 2 mm sieve and inspect the catch. For rodent hair, spread calyces on a white tray and look for thin, dark hairs under bright light. Stones and metal bits are heavierâshake the bag and listen for rattling.

Chemical contaminants are harder to see. Pesticide residue can cause a bitter taste or burning sensation in the throat. If calyces taste bitter or make your tongue numb, reject them. Heavy metals from drying on contaminated surfaces (like old batteries or painted metal) can be present. Buy from trusted suppliers who dry on clean racks. A simple field test for excess sulphur (used as preservative) is to smell for a sharp, matchâlike odour. If present, wash calyces in warm water before use, but better to avoid.

Always buy from a supplier who allows you to inspect the batch. Take a 500 g sample, perform the water test, smell test, and visual inspection. If any test fails, walk away. Your concentrateâs safety and reputation depend on clean raw materials.

lessons.title: Proper storage to prevent mold and insect damage
lessons.body:
Even perfectly dried calyces can spoil if stored wrong. The enemies are moisture, heat, light, insects, and rodents. Use airtight containers: clean plastic drums with tight lids, glass jars, or heavyâduty polythene bags sealed with heat or tape. Never use open sacks or bags that have held fertiliser, cement, or chemicalsâresidual odours and toxins penetrate the calyces. If using jute bags, line them with foodâgrade plastic and tie tightly. Store in a cool, dark room. Ideal temperature is 15â25Â°C; above 30Â°C, colour fades and insects breed faster. Keep away from walls and floorâplace on wooden pallets or shelves at least 30 cm off the ground.

Moisture control is key. Add a desiccant sachet (silica gel) to each container if you live in a humid area. You can make a cheap desiccant by baking rice or maize in a dry pan until brittle, then wrapping in a cloth and placing in the container. Check monthly. If you see condensation inside the lid, your calyces are reabsorbing moisture. Remove them, reâdry in sun for 2â3 hours, and repack with fresh desiccant.

Insect prevention: before storing, freeze calyces for 48 hours in a deep freezer. This kills eggs and larvae. Then store with natural repellents: dried neem leaves, cloves, or black pepper in small cloth bags. Do not let repellents touch the calyces directly. Inspect every 2 weeks for the first 2 months. Look for fine dust (frass), webbing, or live beetles. If you find insects, reâdry and reâfreeze the entire batch. For rodents, use metal containers or place traps around the storage area. Never use rat poison near food.

Label each container with date and source. Use oldest stock first. Properly stored calyces last 12â18 months without quality loss. After 18 months, colour and flavour decline. Plan your purchases so you use stock within one year.

lessons.title: Supplier evaluation and bulk purchasing strategies
lessons.body:
Your business depends on reliable suppliers. Start by identifying at least three potential suppliers: local farmers, market aggregators, and cooperatives. Visit their drying and storage facilities. A good supplier dries on raised racks, not on the ground; stores in clean, dry rooms; and allows you to inspect any batch. Ask about harvest date, variety, and drying method. Avoid suppliers who cannot answer basic questions or who refuse inspection. Check references from other buyers. In Nigeria, major hibiscus producing states include Kano, Jigawa, Katsina, and Sokoto. In Senegal, the SinÃ©âSaloum region. In Kenya, around Kisumu. Buy directly from farmers or cooperatives to cut costs and ensure traceability.

When evaluating a sample, request 1 kg from the top, middle, and bottom of the bag. Perform the water test, smell test, and moisture check. Look for consistent colour and aroma. A good supplier will have uniform batches. Ask for a price per kilogram and negotiate based on quality. Premium calyces (deep red, low moisture, no foreign matter) command higher prices but give better yield. Calculate yield: 1 kg dried calyces yields about 8â10 litres of concentrate. So if you pay â¦2,000/kg and sell concentrate at â¦1,500/litre, your raw material cost is â¦200â250 per litre. That leaves room for profit.

For bulk purchasing, buy during harvest season (NovemberâFebruary in West Africa) when prices are lowest. Buy at least 50â100 kg if you have storage. Pool orders with other producers to get volume discounts. Always pay a fair priceâunderpaying leads to poor quality or adulteration. Build longâterm relationships: offer advance payment or a premium for consistent quality. Sign a simple contract specifying quality parameters, delivery dates, and penalties for adulteration. Keep records of each supplierâs performance. Over time, you will know who is reliable. Never buy from more than 3â4 suppliers to keep quality control manageable. Always have a backup supplier in case of crop failure.

lessons.title: Handsâon: grading and sorting hibiscus calyces
lessons.body:
Grading and sorting turn a mixed batch into premium product. Start with a clean, dry table or mat. Spread a 5 kg batch in a thin layer. Wear clean cotton gloves to avoid oils from your hands. Work under bright light. You will create three grades: Grade A (premium), Grade B (standard), and Grade C (reject). Grade A: whole, deep red calyces, uniform size, no foreign matter, no insect damage. Grade B: slightly broken or paler calyces, minor foreign matter (less than 2%). Grade C: brown, mouldy, insectâinfested, or heavily contaminatedâdiscard or sell for nonâfood use.

Begin by removing large debris: leaves, stems, stones, and twigs. Then sift through a 2 mm sieve to remove sand and dust. Next, pick out discoloured calyces. A simple colour chart helps: hold a calyx against a printed colour swatch (deep red, medium red, pale red). Train your eye to spot offâcolours. For insect damage, look for tiny holes, webbing, or live insects. Discard any calyx with holes. For mould, look for white or green patchesâdiscard immediately and do not mix with good calyces. Use a small magnet to pick up metal bits. Finally, check for rodent hair by spreading a sample on white paper and inspecting under a lamp.

After sorting, weigh each grade. A typical 5 kg batch yields: Grade A 3 kg (60%), Grade B 1.5 kg (30%), Grade C 0.5 kg (10%). Pack grades separately in labelled containers. Grade A fetches the highest price and is best for your own concentrate. Grade B can be used for lowerâpriced products or sold to other processors. Grade C should be composted or sold for dye extraction. Record the yield percentagesâthis helps you calculate how much raw material to buy. For example, if you need 10 kg of Grade A, you must buy about 16.7 kg of unsorted calyces (10 Ã· 0.6).

Practice sorting with a timer: aim to sort 1 kg in 15â20 minutes. Speed comes with experience. Always clean your workspace between batches to avoid crossâcontamination. Proper grading ensures consistent quality in your final concentrate.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Grading and Sorting Hibiscus Calyces for Premium Zobo/Sobolo Concentrate

In the African hibiscus value chain â from Kano and Katsina in Nigeria to Sudan's Nile corridor, Senegal's ThiÃ¨s region, and Tanzania's Morogoro highlands â the difference between a profitable zobo concentrate operation and a marginal one often comes down to what happens on the sorting table. Buyers of dried calyces, whether they are local aggregators, export traders, or concentrate processors, pay premiums for consistent color, low foreign matter, and predictable moisture. A well-run grading and sorting line can lift farmgate-to-FOB margins by 20â40% because it converts mixed-quality harvests into standardized lots that meet buyer specifications.

This practical reference covers the hands-on steps for grading and sorting Hibiscus sabdariffa calyces, the quality parameters that matter commercially, and how to build a repeatable sorting protocol that protects your concentrate's color, flavor, and shelf life.

Why Grading Matters Commercially

Hibiscus calyces are traded on visual and analytical specifications. Export-grade Nigerian and Sudanese calyces typically require: whole or cut calyces, deep red to purple color, moisture â¤ 12%, foreign matter â¤ 1%, and freedom from mold and live insects. Concentrate processors care about color density (anthocyanin content), acidity, and extract yield â all of which degrade with poor sorting and storage. Grading is not cosmetic; it is the first step in quality assurance and the main lever for price differentiation.

Step-by-Step Grading and Sorting Protocol

1. Receiving and lot identification. Assign each incoming batch a lot number tied to farm, harvest date, and drying method. Sample 5â10% of bags using a grain probe or scoop. Never mix lots before grading â traceability is what allows you to negotiate with premium buyers.

2. Visual color sorting. Spread calyces on a clean, light-colored table or conveyor. Remove pale pink, brown, blackened, or bleached calyces. Target a uniform deep red-purple. Color is the single strongest predictor of anthocyanin content and buyer acceptance.

3. Foreign matter removal. Hand-pick stones, sand, twigs, leaves, and seed capsules. Use a 4â6 mm sieve to separate undersized fragments and dust. Magnetic traps or manual inspection remove metal fragments from mechanical threshers.

4. Defect removal. Discard calyces with mold (white, green, or black fuzz), insect holes, webbing, or frass. Moldy calyces can carry mycotoxins and must never enter the food chain.

5. Size grading. Use slotted or round-hole sieves to separate whole calyces from cut and broken pieces. Whole calyces command higher prices for tea and export; broken pieces are acceptable for concentrate extraction but should be sold as a separate grade.

6. Moisture verification. Test each lot with a calibrated moisture meter. Target 10â12%. Above 12% invites mold; below 8% makes calyces brittle and increases breakage. Record readings per lot.

7. Final QC and packaging. Weigh, label, and seal in food-grade woven polypropylene or jute bags with inner liners. Store on pallets in a dry, ventilated warehouse away from walls and floors.

Sources: Adapted from IITA post-harvest handling guides for African leafy and calyx crops; NEPC export documentation; field benchmarks from Nigerian and Sudanese hibiscus aggregators.

â  SAFETY WARNING â MOLD AND MYCOTOXINS

Never attempt to "clean," wash, or blend moldy hibiscus calyces into a food or beverage product. Moldy calyces may contain mycotoxins (e.g., aflatoxins, ochratoxin A) that are heat-stable and can cause serious illness or liver damage. Discard moldy material immediately and away from food streams. Workers handling suspect lots should wear dust masks and gloves. If a lot smells musty or shows white, green, or black fuzz, reject the entire lot â do not salvage.

Building a Repeatable Grading Protocol

Standardize your grading with written specifications, trained sorters, and lot-level records. Train sorters using reference samples â physical examples of premium, standard, and reject calyces â so decisions are consistent across shifts. Calibrate moisture meters monthly against an oven-drying reference method. Keep a simple log per lot: origin, weight in, weight out per grade, moisture, and defects found. This data becomes your negotiating tool with buyers and your early warning for supplier problems.

For concentrate producers, grading directly affects extraction economics. Cleaner, well-sorted calyces yield more color and flavor per kilogram, reduce filtration problems, and extend shelf life of the final concentrate. A 5% improvement in sorting efficiency often pays for itself within one harvest season.

Quick Reference Checklist

  • Assign a lot number to every incoming batch before grading.
  • Sort on a clean, light-colored surface for accurate color judgment.
  • Remove all moldy, insect-damaged, and discolored calyces â never salvage.
  • Verify moisture with a calibrated meter; target 10â12%.
  • Use sieves to separate whole calyces from broken pieces and dust.
  • Wear gloves and dust masks when handling suspect or dusty lots.
  • Record weight, moisture, and defects per lot for traceability.
  • Store graded bags on pallets in a dry, ventilated, pest-controlled warehouse.

quiz.q: What is the ideal moisture content for dried hibiscus calyces?
quiz.explanation: 10â12% moisture prevents mould and insect damage while keeping calyces intact.

quiz.q: Which drying method gives the best colour retention?
options: B) Drying on a corrugated iron roof
C) Using a solar dryer at 50â60Â°C
D) Drying in a closed plastic bag
quiz.explanation: A solar dryer reaches 50â60Â°C and dries quickly, preserving deep red colour.

quiz.q: How can you test for sand adulteration in hibiscus calyces?
options: B) Put in water and look for sediment
quiz.explanation: Sand sinks in water while calyces float, making sediment easy to spot.

quiz.q: What does a musty smell in dried calyces indicate?
quiz.explanation: Musty smell is a clear sign of mould growth from improper drying or storage.

quiz.q: Which of these is a natural insect repellent for stored calyces?
quiz.explanation: Dried neem leaves, cloves, or black pepper repel insects without contaminating the calyces.

quiz.q: What is the first step before storing dried calyces to kill insect eggs?
quiz.explanation: Freezing for 48 hours kills eggs and larvae without affecting quality.

quiz.q: How many litres of concentrate does 1 kg of dried calyces typically yield?
quiz.explanation: 1 kg dried calyces yields about 8â10 litres of concentrate, depending on recipe.

quiz.q: When is the best time to buy hibiscus calyces in bulk in West Africa?
options: D) Any time, prices are constant
quiz.explanation: Harvest season in West Africa is NovemberâFebruary, when prices are lowest.

quiz.q: What does a bright red instant colour in cold water suggest?
quiz.explanation: Natural hibiscus releases colour slowly; instant bright red indicates artificial dye.

quiz.q: Which grade of calyces is best for making premium concentrate?
quiz.explanation: Grade A has whole, deep red calyces with no foreign matter, giving the best colour and flavour.

quiz.q: What is the ideal temperature range for storing dried hibiscus?
quiz.explanation: 15â25Â°C is cool and dark, preventing colour fade and insect breeding.

quiz.q: How can you test if calyces are dry enough without a meter?
options: A) They feel soft and pliable
B) They crumble and crack when squeezed
quiz.explanation: Dry calyces crumble and crack; wet ones clump or feel clammy.

quiz.q: Which of these is a common adulterant in hibiscus?
quiz.explanation: Sawdust, sand, and dried tomato peel are cheap fillers used to increase weight.

quiz.q: What should you do if you find mould on some calyces in a batch?
options: B) Discard the mouldy ones and do not mix
quiz.explanation: Mould spreads and produces toxins; discard mouldy calyces and never mix with good ones.

quiz.q: How long can properly stored dried hibiscus last?
quiz.explanation: With proper drying and storage, quality lasts 12â18 months.

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of a desiccant in storage?
quiz.explanation: Desiccants like silica gel absorb moisture to prevent mould growth.

quiz.q: Which test helps detect added red dye?
options: A) Rub a wet calyx on white paper
quiz.explanation: Natural colour leaves a faint pink stain; dye leaves a strong, unnatural red streak.

quiz.q: What is the ideal drying temperature for hibiscus in a solar dryer?
quiz.explanation: 50â60Â°C dries quickly while preserving colour and flavour.

quiz.q: How can you check for rodent hair in a batch?
options: B) Spread on white paper under bright light
quiz.explanation: Rodent hairs are thin and dark; they show up clearly on white paper under good light.

quiz.q: What is the typical yield of Grade A calyces from a 5 kg unsorted batch?
quiz.explanation: About 60% of a batch is Grade A, so 5 kg yields roughly 3 kg.

quiz.q: Which of these is a sign of insect infestation?
options: B) Fine webbing and small holes
quiz.explanation: Webbing, holes, and frass (dust) indicate insect activity.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid storing hibiscus in fertiliser bags?
options: B) Residual chemicals can contaminate the calyces
quiz.explanation: Fertiliser bags may contain toxic residues that leach into the calyces.

quiz.q: What is the best time of day to harvest hibiscus calyces?
options: A) Early morning after dew dries
quiz.explanation: Early morning after dew dries avoids moisture and heat damage.

quiz.q: How can you estimate moisture content using an oven?
options: B) Dry 100 g at 105Â°C for 2 hours and weigh
C) Soak in water and weigh
quiz.explanation: Weight loss after oven drying indicates moisture content; over 12 g loss per 100 g is too high.

quiz.q: Which of these is a good supplier practice?
quiz.explanation: Raised racks prevent contamination and ensure even drying.

quiz.q: What does a bitter taste in calyces indicate?
quiz.explanation: Bitter taste can mean pesticide residue or other chemical contaminants.

quiz.q: How often should you inspect stored calyces for insects?
options: B) Every 2 weeks for first 2 months
C) Only when you use them
quiz.explanation: Frequent inspection catches infestations early before they spread.

quiz.q: What is the first step in grading hibiscus calyces?
quiz.explanation: Remove leaves, stems, stones, and twigs before finer sorting.

quiz.q: Which grade of calyces should be discarded or sold for nonâfood use?
quiz.explanation: Grade C has mould, insect damage, or heavy contamination and is unsafe for food.

quiz.q: What is a simple field test for excess sulphur preservative?
quiz.explanation: Sulphur gives a sharp, matchâlike smell that indicates excessive preservative use.
